summary: For ages 8–9: multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10 (10–90) by reasoning from a known fact scaled by ten — 7×30 = 7×(3×10) = (7×3)×10 = 21 tens = 210 — using place value and the associative property. The objective is the reasoning, not the 'add a zero' trick: learners should understand multiplying by 10 as making a number ten times larger so its digits shift one place left, which is why 210 ends in a zero (the ones place empties). This understanding survives the later move to decimals, where 'add a zero' fails (0.7×10 = 7, not 0.70), and powers estimation (234×5 ≈ 200×5) and multiplication by multiples of 100/1000.
misconceptions: Over-relying on 'add a zero' as a rule without understanding, which later misfires with decimals (0.7×30).
Multiplying the wrong part (7×30 as 21 rather than 210) — losing the place-value scaling.
Adding an extra or too few zeros through miscounting places.
Not connecting 7×30 to the known fact 7×3, so it's computed from scratch.
Confusing multiplying by a multiple of ten with adding tens.

activities.title: Scaling a known fact by ten with place-value counters
steps: Build the known fact 7×3 as an array of 21 single counters (or draw them).
Replace each single counter with a rod of ten, stating aloud 'now there are 21 tens'.
Regroup the 21 tens: exchange ten tens for one hundred, repeat, ending with 2 hundreds and 1 ten.
Record the result on a place-value chart (hundreds | tens | ones) and read it as 210.
Say the full reasoning chain: '7×3 = 21, so 7×30 = 21 tens = 210, because 30 is 3 tens.'
Repeat for 5×60 (5×6 = 30, so 5×60 = 30 tens = 300) and 3×40 (3×4 = 12, so 3×40 = 12 tens = 120), each time naming the known single-digit fact first.
activities.insight: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 is multiplying by the single-digit fact and then by ten; the extra zero in the product is the result of every digit shifting one place left as the amount becomes ten times larger, not a zero 'stuck on the end'.

activities.title: Why 'add a zero' is not the real rule
steps: On a place-value chart, place 7 in the ones column, then slide it one column left to make 70; describe what happened to the digit.
Do the same with 21: slide it one column left so the ones place becomes empty and a 0 fills it, giving 210.
Now try 0.7×10 on the same chart: slide 0.7 one column left to get 7 — notice no zero was added.
State in your own words why '×10 shifts digits one place left' is safer than 'add a zero'.
(Optional extension, once the tens pattern feels secure) Predict and check 7×300 using the same idea: 7×3 = 21, shifted two places = 2100.
activities.insight: Multiplying by ten always shifts digits one place to the left; for whole numbers this shows up as a trailing zero, but the shift — not the zero itself — is the real rule, which is why it still works for decimals.

activities.title: Using tens facts to estimate
steps: Estimate 6×43 by rounding 43 to 40 and computing 6×40 = 240 (6×4 = 24, so 6×40 = 24 tens = 240), explaining the reasoning.

(Optional extension, once the tens case is secure) Estimate 234×5 by rounding 234 to 200 and computing 200×5 = 1000 (2×5 = 10, so 200×5 = 10 hundreds = 1000), using the same known-fact-then-scale reasoning.
Compare each estimate to the exact answer (6×43 = 258; 234×5 = 1170) and say whether the estimate is high or low and roughly by how much.
Make up one estimation of your own using a multiple of ten and justify it.
activities.insight: Multiplying by a multiple of ten (and, by the same reasoning, a multiple of a hundred) lets you quickly bound or approximate a larger product, which checks whether an exact answer is reasonable.

activities.title: Spot and explain the error
steps: Decide whether each worked example is correct: 7×30 = 21; 5×60 = 300; 8×40 = 32; 9×80 = 720.
For any that are wrong, say exactly what went wrong (e.g. multiplied the tens as ones, or dropped/added a zero).
Rewrite each incorrect one with the full reasoning chain to make it correct.
Explain in words why 5×60 = 300 ends in a zero.
activities.insight: Common slips — multiplying the tens digit as ones, or miscounting zeros — can be caught by checking against the known-fact-times-ten chain.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to work out 7 × 30 and 6 × 40 in their head, saying how they did it. Watch whether they use the known fact (7×3) and reason about tens, or whether they just 'add a zero' without understanding — then probe by asking what 7 × 30 has to do with 7 × 3.
checkAnswer: 210 and 240. The teacher watches for the child reasoning '7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210' — using the single-digit fact and scaling by ten — rather than a disconnected zero-adding rule.
